{"id": "a750d030-2a45-49af-b898-819f2c6246e9", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_cEJbRpT2QamhCVu4xWoHcO", "content": [{"text": "{"iso8601":"2026-10-01T18:26:48.723349+00:00","unix":1790879208.723,"day_of_week":"Thursday"}"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_WoGiNZOqFvqpClGMAdhrxP", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation
     3	description: Use this skill for GPU training or inference clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or
     4	  EKS), ParallelCluster, or self-managed EC2/EKS GPU instances. It adds three things.
     5	  First, a GPU evidence coverage audit that proves per node whether kernel Xid logs and
     6	  HyperPod health-agent detections were actually arriving, hour by hour, so "no errors
     7	  found" is never reported from a silent log. Second, a node verdict (replace, reboot,
     8	  or leave alone) against an explicit evidence bar, so an application Xid is never
     9	  headlined as hardware. Third, a pre-flight readiness check before a long run, covering
     10	  Capacity Block or training plan end time versus run length, spare capacity to replace
     11	  a failed node, NodeRecovery, deep health checks, EFA, log coverage, idle reserved
     12	  GPUs. Activate on Xid or ECC errors, slow training or FSx for Lustre slowness on a GPU
     13	  cluster, NCCL hangs or TCP fallback, NVLink or Fabric Manager errors, nodes in Failure
     14	  or Pending, nodes terminating at once, or "is my cluster ready for a multi-day run".
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: nzuresh
     17	  version: "1.0.3"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA, Chat tasks"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, AWS ParallelCluster, Amazon EC2, Amazon FSx for Lustre, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Amazon EKS, AWS Health"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Machine Learning, GenAI, High Performance Computing"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# GPU Cluster Evidence, Readiness, and Fault Verdicts
     24	
     25	For GPU clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or EKS), AWS ParallelCluster, and self-managed
     26	EC2 or EKS. Generic investigation finds the obvious signals; this skill adds what it gets
     27	wrong: silent evidence, wrong-headline hardware verdicts, and predictable failures before a
     28	long run. **Read-only.** Never reboot, replace, update, or delete anything, and never read
     29	training data, checkpoints, or model weights.
     30	
     31	## Critical rules R1 to R10 (apply in every mode, in this order)
     32	
     33	R1. **Answer in one pass, and always leave room to answer.** In chat, do not stop to ask a
     34	   question and do not hand off to a separate investigation before answering. If an input is
     35	   missing, use the default (impact window: last 24 hours; run length: evaluate 24, 48, and
     36	   72 hours), state the assumption, and mark dependent checks `Needs input`. For "slow" or
     37	   performance questions with no time given, use the last 72 hours. Offer follow-ups only
     38	   after the answer.
     39	   **Budget the evidence gathering so the answer always gets written.** An investigation that
     40	   runs out of room before it reports is worth nothing to the operator, and it is worse than a
     41	   partial answer because it looks like a failure rather than a finding. So: collect the
     42	   mandatory evidence for the mode first (R2, R4, R5, and for Mode P the P1 to P6 core), then
     43	   write the report. Pick up the optional checks only with what is left. If you notice you are
     44	   deep into tool calls and have not yet produced an answer, **stop collecting and report what
     45	   you have**, marking everything unreached as `Not checked` with the call that would close
     46	   it. Never end a turn with evidence gathered and no verdict.
     47	R2. **Inventory and capability profile.** HyperPod: `sagemaker.DescribeCluster` and
     48	   `ListClusterNodes` (paginate). Read `NodeProvisioningMode` from `DescribeCluster`: if it is
     49	   `Continuous`, also pull `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` for the window (see rule R11), which
     50	   is the only timeline source that survives broken log delivery. On any other value the call
     51	   is unsupported and must be skipped, not retried.
     52	   EC2/ParallelCluster/EKS: `ec2.DescribeInstances`. For every
     53	   GPU instance type: `ec2.DescribeInstanceTypes` (strip HyperPod `ml.`): GPU count,
     54	   `EfaSupported`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces`; per EC2 node, attached `efa`/`efa-only` interfaces.
     55	   Report `<attached> of <max>`, where attached = interfaces with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     56	   `efa-only` (the primary ENA interface does not count unless it is `efa`). HyperPod nodes
     57	   are not visible to `DescribeInstances`: say so. On NVSwitch types, search every log source
     58	   found under rule R4 for `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` before saying it is not confirmed.
     59	R3. **Node identity survives replacement.** A HyperPod reboot keeps the instance ID; a replace
     60	   gives the node a **new instance ID in the same instance group**, so the current ID will
     61	   never appear in the replace request. Query CloudTrail **by event name, not by instance
     62	   ID**: `cloudtrail.LookupEvents` with `LookupAttributes=[{AttributeKey: EventName,
     63	   AttributeValue: BatchReplaceClusterNodes}]`, then again for `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     64	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `UpdateCluster`, with `StartTime` = window start minus 6
     65	   hours and `EndTime` = now as full ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, paginating with `NextToken`.
     66	   Keep events whose `requestParameters.clusterName` is this cluster. A `nodeIds` entry
     67	   that is not in the current `ListClusterNodes` output was replaced; the instance group
     68	   whose node has a `LaunchTime` just after that event is the replaced group. That operator
     69	   or automatic call is the explanation for the node going `Pending` (Branch E), not hardware.
     70	R4. **Find every log source by substring, not prefix.** Call `logs.DescribeLogGroups` with
     71	   `logGroupNamePattern` (case-sensitive substring) = the cluster name, then again for
     72	   `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`, `journal`, and `gpu`, paginating with `nextToken`. Never
     73	   search only `/aws/parallelcluster` or `/aws/sagemaker` prefixes: customer pipelines use
     74	   other names (for example `/aws/<pipeline>/<cluster>/kernel`). Evaluate every source found.
     75	R5. **Prove coverage before any "no errors".** For each node and source: find the stream that
     76	   carries `kernel:` lines, then bin **that exact stream** by hour across the window padded by
     77	   one hour. **Always name the evidence you used: quote the full log group name and the exact
     78	   log stream name for every node in the coverage table, and again in the answer text.** A
     79	   coverage claim without the group and stream it rests on is not auditable, so the operator
     80	   cannot re-run it. Any empty hour means `Not observable` for that hour. First and last event times
     81	   are not proof, and the time of the **last `kernel:` line** is not when logging stopped:
     82	   a healthy kernel goes quiet. Liveness comes only from the hourly bins of all lines in
     83	   that stream. A node is `Measured` if one source passes. HyperPod: a missing
     84	   `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<group>/<instance-id>` stream means `No HMA detections`
     85	   when the cluster log group is otherwise live. NCCL transport with no `NCCL INFO` lines
     86	   anywhere is `Not observable`; never infer it from the instance type.
     87	R5a. **Name every resource you looked at, by ID.** A finding the operator cannot re-run is
     88	   not a finding. Whatever you analysed, put its identifier in the answer: the FSx file system
     89	   (`fs-...`) behind any storage claim, the instance IDs (`i-...`) behind any node claim, the
     90	   cluster name, the capacity reservation (`cr-...`) behind any capacity claim, and the log
     91	   group and stream behind any log claim as R5 already requires. "The file system was
     92	   saturated" or "the metrics looked fine" names nothing and cannot be checked. This applies
     93	   to the resource you cleared as much as the one you blamed, since ruling something out is
     94	   only useful if the reader knows what was ruled out.
     95	R6. **Verdict per node, headline to match.** `REPLACE`, `REBOOT`, `LEAVE ALONE`, `MONITOR`, or
     96	   `NOT OBSERVABLE`, against the evidence bar in `references/incident-branches.md` (Step 4b).
     97	   Application-class Xids (for example 13, 31) or HMA `reason: XidUserAppError` with the node
     98	   `Running` is `LEAVE ALONE`. Never headline "hardware error" unless the verdict is `REPLACE`
     99	   or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds.
     100	R7. **Label every cause** `Proven` (measured signal on the affected node, before the failure,
     101	   nothing competing) or `Hypothesis (to validate)` with the one confirming measurement. A
     102	   spike at the same time is correlation. FSx without a saturated metric is not a proven cause.
     103	   Only a `Proven` cause may be called the root cause, in the headline or in a branch table.
     104	   Otherwise write `Leading hypothesis: <cause>`, or `Root cause: Not observable` when the
     105	   deciding evidence is missing (for example a dead control-plane log). Never write "Proven
     106	   mechanism" for something whose trigger or removal path you did not observe.
     107	   Utilization metrics from FSx (`NetworkThroughputUtilization`, `DiskIopsUtilization`, and
     108	   similar) and `GPUPowerUtilization` are already percent from 0 to 100: a value of `0.9` is
     109	   0.9 percent. Quote the raw value with a percent sign.
     110	R8. **Recovery questions** always state three things: whether automatic node recovery is on
     111	   (`NodeRecovery`), what it does (reboot or replace the node), and that the **job** resumes
     112	   only with checkpoints plus the orchestrator's auto-resume (Slurm on HyperPod:
     113	   `srun --auto-resume=1`).
     114	R9. **Capacity Blocks** begin terminating instances 30 minutes before the end time (60 for
     115	   UltraServers); blocks end at 11:30 UTC and termination starts at 11:00 UTC on the last day.
     116	   For a planned run, write out: usable until = end time minus the lead time; run end = start
     117	   plus run length; hours covered = usable until minus start. Give every value as a full UTC
     118	   date and time, and check the latest safe start is not already in the past.
     119	R10. **Rule out the frequent non-GPU causes** in `references/cluster-edge-cases.md` before
     120	   blaming hardware: subnet IP or network interface exhaustion, ParallelCluster bootstrap
     121	   failures and protected mode, EFA nodes in a public subnet, a Capacity Block not yet
     122	   active, and the FSx maintenance window. HyperPod does not export system metrics to
     123	   CloudWatch, so HyperPod GPU activity is `Not observable` there.
     124	R11. **When the logs are dead, ask the control plane.** On a HyperPod cluster with
     125	   `NodeProvisioningMode = Continuous`, `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` gives you a node and
     126	   cluster timeline that owes nothing to a log agent, so it keeps answering when a stream has
     127	   gone silent or a node has disappeared. Filter the window with `EventTimeAfter` and
     128	   `EventTimeBefore`, narrow with `NodeId` or `InstanceGroupName`, sort with
     129	   `SortBy=EventTime`, and page through `NextToken`. Where a `Description` is not
     130	   self-explanatory, `DescribeClusterEvent` has the detail. Note that the response has no
     131	   severity or level field at all, so any grouping you apply is your own and should be
     132	   described that way. If `NodeProvisioningMode` is anything other than `Continuous` the call
     133	   is not supported; write `ListClusterEvents not supported` in the coverage table and carry
     134	   on. What you must not do is report a dead log as "no events" without either trying this
     135	   source or saying it was unavailable.
     136	
     137	## Pick the mode
     138	
     139	| The user asks | Mode | Steps to run |
     140	|---------------|------|--------------|
     141	| Something failed, hung, slowed, or lost nodes | **I: Incident** | Steps 1 to 7 |
     142	| "Were there GPU errors?", "Can I trust the logs?" | **C: Coverage audit** | Steps 1 to 3, then 6 and 7 |
     143	| "Is the cluster ready for a long run?", Capacity Block ending | **P: Pre-flight** | Steps 1 to 3, then 5P, 6 and 7 |
     144	
     145	## Workflow checklist
     146	
     147	Work through these in order and tick each one as it completes. Skip only the steps the
     148	mode table excludes. Every step below has a matching `## Step N` section with its detail.
     149	
     150	- [ ] Step 1: Scope the request: account, region, cluster or instance IDs, impact window
     151	- [ ] Step 2: Build the inventory, capability profile, and one ordered timeline
     152	- [ ] Step 3: Prove GPU log coverage per node before looking for errors
     153	- [ ] Step 4: Classify each fault and give every node a verdict
     154	- [ ] Step 5: Pull metrics and settle the root-cause branch
     155	- [ ] Step 5P: Score pre-flight checks P1 to P16 (Mode P only, replaces Steps 4 and 5)
     156	- [ ] Step 6: Write the report in the required format
     157	- [ ] Step 7: Self-check the finished output, then present it
     158	
     159	## Step 1: Scope
     160	
     161	Account, region, cluster name or instance IDs, workload, impact window (default last 24 hours,
     162	stated). Classify the symptom to pick a starting branch (Step 5), but collect evidence for all.
     163	
     164	## Step 2: Inventory and timeline
     165	
     166	Load [references/inventory-and-timeline.md](references/inventory-and-timeline.md) for the
     167	inventory API calls and the eight timeline sources, and
     168	[references/cluster-edge-cases.md](references/cluster-edge-cases.md) for the frequent non-GPU
     169	causes to rule out under rule R10:
     170	
     171	```
     172	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/inventory-and-timeline.md")
     173	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/cluster-edge-cases.md")
     174	```
     175	
     176	Build one ordered timeline for the window plus 30 minutes each side: node state, HMA
     177	detections, Xids, AWS Health, EC2 status and scheduled events, Capacity Block and training plan
     178	end times, and CloudTrail cluster changes (rule R3).
     179	
     180	## Step 3: Coverage audit
     181	
     182	Load [references/coverage-audit.md](references/coverage-audit.md) for the log-source discovery
     183	and hourly coverage queries, and
     184	[references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md](references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md) for NCCL transport, NVLink and
     185	NVSwitch, and EFA signals:
     186	
     187	```
     188	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/coverage-audit.md")
     189	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md")
     190	```
     191	
     192	Produce the coverage table and the node capability and fabric table for every affected node.
     193	Every row names the full log group name and the exact log stream name that row's verdict rests
     194	on, so the operator can re-run the same query. Where no stream carries kernel lines, say which
     195	groups you searched and that none did.
     196	
     197	## Step 4: Classify faults and give node verdicts
     198	
     199	Load [references/xid-triage.md](references/xid-triage.md) for the Xid catalog and per-code
     200	verdicts, and [references/incident-branches.md](references/incident-branches.md) for the node
     201	verdict evidence bar and branches A to F:
     202	
     203	```
     204	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/xid-triage.md")
     205	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/incident-branches.md")
     206	```
     207	
     208	## Step 5: Metrics and root-cause branch
     209	
     210	Load [references/signals-and-thresholds.md](references/signals-and-thresholds.md) for metric
     211	names, dimensions, and thresholds:
     212	
     213	```
     214	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/signals-and-thresholds.md")
     215	```
     216	
     217	Pull FSx (correct dimensions per metric), GPU activity (`AWS/EC2` `GPUPowerUtilization`, unit
     218	Percent, or `CWAgent`), and EFA counters, then evaluate branches A (hardware), B (capacity
     219	lifecycle), C (storage), D (NCCL, NVLink/NVSwitch, EFA), E (cluster change), and F (application,
     220	only after A to E are ruled out), as defined in `incident-branches.md`. Recommend operator
     221	actions only.
     222	
     223	## Step 5P: Pre-flight readiness (Mode P)
     224	
     225	Load [references/preflight.md](references/preflight.md) for pre-flight checks P1 to P16:
     226	
     227	```
     228	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/preflight.md")
     229	```
     230	
     231	Score checks P1 to P16. Lead with FAIL, then RISK. In Mode P this step replaces
     232	Steps 4 and 5.
     233	
     234	**Work the core first, then extend.** All sixteen checks together cost more tool calls than
     235	a single answer usually has room for, and a readiness question with no verdict is a failed
     236	answer however much evidence sits behind it (see R1). So run them in two passes.
     237	
     238	The core, which decides whether the run can start at all:
     239	
     240	| Check | Question it settles |
     241	|-------|---------------------|
     242	| P1 | Does the Capacity Block or training plan outlast the run? |
     243	| P2 | Is there an extension, if it does not? |
     244	| P3 | Is there a spare node to replace a failure? |
     245	| P4 | Is `NodeRecovery` on? |
     246	| P5 | Are deep health checks enabled? |
     247	| P6 | Is GPU error logging arriving, so a failure during the run is visible? |
     248	
     249	Write the readiness verdict as soon as those six are scored. P7 to P16 then refine it, and
     250	each one you reach can only add a `RISK`, never change a `FAIL` already found in the core.
     251	Anything you do not reach is reported `Not checked` with the call that would settle it, which
     252	is an honest answer; silence is not. If the core itself is incomplete, say which part and
     253	give the verdict you can support.
     254	
     255	## Step 6: Report
     256	
     257	Load [references/report-format.md](references/report-format.md) for the report template and its rules:
     258	
     259	```
     260	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/report-format.md")
     261	```
     262	
     263	## Step 7: Self-check before presenting
     264	
     265	Before showing the answer to the user, re-read your own draft and verify each of these.
     266	Fix the draft where a check fails; do not present an output that fails one.
     267	
     268	- [ ] Every "no errors found" statement is backed by a node whose coverage you proved in
     269	      Step 3. If coverage was not proven, the wording is `Not observable`, not healthy.
     270	- [ ] Every coverage row names its full log group and exact log stream (rule R5). A coverage
     271	      claim with no named source is not auditable and must be fixed before presenting.
     272	- [ ] Stream names appear as the service writes them, not paraphrased. Search your own draft
     273	      for phrases like "the HMA log stream" or "the health agent log" and replace each with
     274	      the real name, for example
     275	      `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<instance-group>/<instance-id>`. This is the easiest
     276	      check to skip in a short answer and the one that most often makes a finding
     277	      unreproducible.
     278	- [ ] Every node verdict still meets the evidence bar that justifies it, re-read from
     279	      [references/incident-branches.md](references/incident-branches.md) Step 4b.
     280	- [ ] The headline matches the verdicts. It does not say "hardware error" unless a verdict
     281	      is `REPLACE` or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds (rule R6).
     282	- [ ] Every cause carries a `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)` label, and anything
     283	      labelled `Proven` has a measured signal on the affected node before the failure
     284	      (rule R7). Nothing unproven is called the root cause.
     285	- [ ] Every percentage came straight from the metric without rescaling (rule R7).
     286	- [ ] Every absent signal is reported as `Not observable` with what to collect, never as
     287	      zero or as healthy.
     288	- [ ] Each recommendation names an operator action, and no mutating API call was made.
     289	- [ ] Every number in the answer can be traced to a call you actually made this run.
     290	- [ ] Every resource you analysed appears by ID (rule R5a): the `fs-...` behind a storage
     291	      claim, the `i-...` behind a node claim, the `cr-...` behind a capacity claim, the
     292	      cluster name, the log group and stream. This holds for resources you cleared, not just
     293	      the one you blamed.
     294	- [ ] **There is an actual answer.** A verdict or root cause is written down, not just
     295	      evidence. If you ran out of room before finishing, the draft still leads with the
     296	      verdict you can support and marks the rest `Not checked` (rule R1).
     297	
     298	State the outcome of this self-check in one line, naming anything you could not verify.
     299	
     300	## Success criteria
     301	
     302	- Coverage table and node capability table for every affected node; no "no errors" without
     303	  proven coverage.
     304	- One verdict per node with a GPU signal; headline consistent with the verdicts.
     305	- Every cause labelled `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)`.
     306	- Replaced nodes matched to the operator or automatic action that replaced them.
     307	- Mode P: P1 to P16 scored.
     308	- No mutating API call was made.
     309

     320	- [FSx for Lustre metrics and dimensions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/fs-metrics.html)

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "I've read the GPU cluster investigation skill. This is a **Mode I (Incident)** investigation: training throughput slowdown on a GPU cluster backed by FSx for Lustre `fs-077c776983688ad76` in us-west-2 (account 111122223333). - Maintenance window `WeeklyMaintenanceStartTime = 4:11:30` → **Thursday 11:30 UTC** (confirmed via datetime: 2026-10-01 and 2026-09-24 at 11:30Z both fall on Thursday).

# NETWORK / EFA / NCCL Branch — Verdict

## Headline
**The network was NOT the bottleneck for the current slowdown. `Hypothesis — rejected`.** The run active during the "last few days" slowdown window was **single-node** (1× p6-b200.48xlarge, 8× B200, intra-node NVLink only), so EFA / inter-node collective traffic is **irrelevant** to it. Separately, the `EFA=NONE` tag is **misleading**: the GPU launch template provisions the **full 8 of 8 EFA interfaces**. No network edge case (subnet IP/ENI exhaustion, public-subnet, routing) was found.

## 1. EFA interface count — "8 of 8 EFA interfaces" (configured)
- GPU compute launch template `lt-025a88cbeaba7b869` (`distributed-training-triage-b200-gpu-p6b20048xlarge`, default v1 and latest v4) defines: 1 primary ENA (device index 0) **+ 8× `InterfaceType: efa-only`** on NetworkCardIndex 0–7.
- `p6-b200.48xlarge` capability (`describe_instance_types`): `EfaSupported=true`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces=8`, `MaximumNetworkCards=8`, 8 GPUs.
- **Verdict: 8 of 8 EFA interfaces configured — EFA is NOT absent.** The cluster-level tag `parallelcluster:networking: EFA=NONE` **contradicts the actual compute launch template** and should not be trusted. `Proven` (from the launch template; live per-instance ENI confirmation was not possible because all GPU nodes are terminated — only the HeadNode `i-01bbde10b04dd4ca8` (t3.medium) is running).

## 2. Node count — SINGLE-NODE during the slowdown window
Established from `AWS/EC2 GPUPowerUtilization` dimension inventory + per-node timelines (CloudTrail is blocked in this environment, so metric/log timelines were used instead):
- **Current run (slowdown window)**: ONLY `i-0ec31e7eff7635265` active, Sep 30 ~21:00 UTC → Oct 1 18:00 UTC. **1 node = single-node.** GPU power is near-idle the whole window (0.013%–0.16% — raw values, already 0–100 scale), i.e. the GPUs were barely doing work.
- **Prior run (Sep 23 16:00 → Sep 27 10:00 UTC)**: `i-0014ff22f2e2f180f` + `i-0be6193831c898671` ran concurrently ~4 days = a **2-node** run (both in subnet 10.0.38.x within the FSx subnet CIDR). A brief Sep 23 burst touched 4 other IDs (`i-0a3cfc5c…`, `i-0190035…`, `i-01ec042d…`, `i-0ce092c23…`) — a short multi-node test.
- **Pivotal point: no EFA only hurts multi-node jobs. The current job is single-node, so network/EFA cannot be its bottleneck.** `Proven`.

## 3. NCCL transport actually observed — **Not observable**
- Searched all compute log groups for exact NCCL strings (`NCCL INFO`, `NCCL WARN`, `NET/OFI`, `NET/Socket`, `Selected Provider is efa`, `Using network`):
  - `/aws/fsx-training/distributed-training-triage-b200/kernel` — 693,669 records scanned, **0 NCCL matches** (only systemd `*.socket` OS noise on the HeadNode stream).

  - `/aws/fsx-training/distributed-training-triage-b200/gpu-health` and `-cf-test-v2/gpu-health` — 0.
  - `/aws/parallelcluster/distributed-training-triage-b200-202608261551` — only bootstrap streams (chef-client, cloud-init, system-messages); no NCCL.
- The active node `i-0ec31e7eff7635265` ships **no kernel/gpu-health/job logs at all** — it only emits GPUPowerUtilization.
- **Per rule R5, NCCL transport is `Not observable`. I do NOT infer "NCCL used EFA" or "fell back to TCP" from the instance type.** (It is moot anyway for a single-node job: there is no inter-node NCCL traffic to carry.)
- To make it observable on a future multi-node run, operator should set: `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET,P2P,SHM,NVLS NCCL_DEBUG_FILE=/fsx/nccl_%h_%p.log` and ship the file, then confirm `NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa` vs `NET/Socket`.

## 4. Network edge cases (R10) — all ruled out
- **Subnet IP exhaustion**: `subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb` (10.0.32.0/20, us-west-2d) has **4,088 available IPs** — ample headroom even for 8-NIC p6-b200 nodes. Not exhausted. `Proven`.
- **Public-subnet EFA trap**: `MapPublicIpOnLaunch=false` and route table `rtb-06fbcc9d96be3c6a7` sends `0.0.0.0/0` to **NAT gateway `nat-090faa2acde0bec78`** (not an IGW). - **FSx**: `fs-077c776983688ad76` (1200 GiB Lustre, maintenance Thu 11:30 UTC) is in the same subnet — storage path is a sibling branch (not mine), noted for the lead.

Re-deriving the timeline for our actual cluster: the two in-scope B200 GPU nodes ran a ~3-day job from Sep 24 to Sep 27, preceded by a brief multi-node burst on Sep 23, with no in-scope GPU node active after Sep 27 11:00 through Oct 1.

I'm noting the FSx subagent's window started exactly when the GPU nodes started, meaning it likely missed the earlier Sep 23 burst that the network/GPU subagents captured — but that's fine since the run of interest started at the window boundary anyway.

Now piecing together the full timeline: a brief 4-instance multi-node GPU test burst occurred Sep 23 at 16:00Z, then the actual 2-node B200 run began Sep 24 at 18:00Z with the FSx staging burst and GPU power sawtoothing to small peaks.

**The real story:** the GPUs ran at **~0.01% power utilization** — healthy but **starved of work**. With storage idle, the network unsaturated, and the GPUs fault-free, the throughput loss originates **upstream in the data-loading / application pipeline**, which the current telemetry cannot observe (no application logs, NCCL debug, or compute-node GPU/CPU metrics were shipped). That's the investigation gap — it can only be closed with job-level instrumentation on a future run, which is exactly what the mitigation enables.

The mitigation proposal (reconcile the EFA signal and verify NCCL selects EFA/OFI at runtime; install NCCL-debug + application-log + GPU/EFA-metric observability via the ParallelCluster config; investigate the CPU-side dataloader; and treat the small SCRATCH_2 FSx as a conditional, scale-only concern) is a deliberately **forward-looking, partial** fix — it doesn't itself restore throughput because the limiting component can't be measured until the observability is in place and a new run executes. **2. Close the GPU/network/application observability gap**

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Reconcile the misleading EFA tag on distributed-training-triage-b200, enable NCCL/GPU/EFA/application observability, and investigate the dataloader pipeline before the next training run

## Reasoning
Storage (FSx fs-077c776983688ad76), network/EFA, and GPU hardware were all cleared with measured evidence. GPUs ran at ~0.01% power utilization (effectively idle) for the entire 2026-09-24→09-27 run, pointing to a bottleneck upstream of all three — most likely the data-loading/application pipeline. No GPU compute node has run since ~2026-09-27 11:00Z. The cluster-level `EFA=NONE` tag is misleading (launch template lt-025a88cbeaba7b869 provisions 8/8 efa-only interfaces), and no NCCL debug, CWAgent EFA counters, DCGM metrics, or application logs were available to pinpoint the dataloader stall directly. This plan is entirely forward-looking: it corrects the misleading tag, turns on the missing observability, and hands off a scoped investigation into the dataloader for the next run.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current launch template tags (including the misleading…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-tags --filters "Name=resource-id,Values=lt-025a88cbeaba7b869" --region us-west-2
```
**Purpose:** Record the current launch template tags (including the misleading EFA=NONE tag) before any change, so the exact prior state can be restored.
**Risks:** None — read-only call

#### 1.2 Confirm both the default (v1) and latest (v4) launch template versions…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-launch-template-versions --launch-template-id lt-025a88cbeaba7b869 --versions $Default $Latest --region us-west-2
```
**Purpose:** Confirm both the default (v1) and latest (v4) launch template versions still provision all 8 efa-only network interfaces before changing anything.
**Risks:** None — read-only call

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Verify no p6-b200 GPU compute node is currently running, so the tag…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=instance-type,Values=p6-b200.48xlarge" --region us-west-2
```
**Purpose:** Verify no p6-b200 GPU compute node is currently running, so the tag correction and config changes carry zero risk of disrupting an active job.

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Eliminate the misleading EFA=NONE signal that caused this investigation…
**Type:** text
Update the ParallelCluster config's Networking.EfaEnabled setting (or re-tag) so the cluster-level tag matches the launch template reality (8/8 efa-only interfaces already provisioned). Re-run pcluster update-cluster or correct the tag directly so operators are not misled by EFA=NONE on a cluster that actually has EFA.
**Purpose:** Eliminate the misleading EFA=NONE signal that caused this investigation to spend time ruling out a network cause that was never really in question.
**Risks:** A pcluster update-cluster can trigger a compute fleet replacement; schedule for a maintenance window with no active job.

#### 3.2 Record an accurate, explicit EFA status tag on the launch template so…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 create-tags --resources lt-025a88cbeaba7b869 --tags Key=EFAStatus,Value=enabled-8of8 --region us-west-2
```
**Purpose:** Record an accurate, explicit EFA status tag on the launch template so future investigations do not have to re-derive it from the raw network interface list.
**Risks:** Tagging is non-destructive and reversible.

#### 3.3 Close the observability gap that prevented this investigation from…
**Type:** text
For the next training job, export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET,P2P,SHM,NVLS NCCL_DEBUG_FILE=/fsx/nccl_%h_%p.log in the Slurm job script, enable CWAgent EFA counters (efa_rdma_write_bytes, efa_rx_dropped, etc.) and DCGM GPU metrics via the ParallelCluster compute node bootstrap, and ship the training application's own logs (dataloader iteration time, batch-fetch latency, queue depth) to CloudWatch Logs.
**Purpose:** Close the observability gap that prevented this investigation from confirming NCCL transport choice, EFA health, or the dataloader as the root cause.
**Risks:** Verbose NCCL_DEBUG logging adds minor I/O overhead; scope to the first few hundred steps of the next run rather than the entire job.
**Advisory:** Without this instrumentation the next slowdown will again be unexplainable at the application layer — treat this as a prerequisite, not an optional nicety.

#### 3.4 Directly test the leading (unconfirmed) hypothesis that the…
**Type:** text
Separately, have the ML engineering team instrument the training job's dataloader (prefetch queue depth, batch generation time, worker count, CPU utilization on compute nodes) since the GPUs were observed at ~0.01% power utilization — healthy but starved of work — for the entire captured run.
**Purpose:** Directly test the leading (unconfirmed) hypothesis that the data-loading/application layer, not AWS infrastructure, is starving the GPUs.
**Advisory:** If dataloader instrumentation also comes back clean, broaden the search to job orchestration/Slurm scheduling or the training script itself.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the new EFAStatus tag is present and the launch template's…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-tags --filters "Name=resource-id,Values=lt-025a88cbeaba7b869" --region us-west-2
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the new EFAStatus tag is present and the launch template's network interface definitions are unchanged (still 8/8 efa-only).

#### 4.2 Ensure the observability gap is genuinely closed, not just configured
**Type:** text
On the next job's first run, confirm the NCCL debug log, CWAgent EFA metrics, and application dataloader logs are actually arriving in CloudWatch before considering observability closed.
**Purpose:** Ensure the observability gap is genuinely closed, not just configured.

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the launch template tag to its pre-change state captured in the…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 create-tags --resources lt-025a88cbeaba7b869 --tags Key=EFAStatus,Value=<previous-value-or-remove> --region us-west-2
```
**Purpose:** Restore the launch template tag to its pre-change state captured in the prepare phase if the new tag breaks any tooling that keys off the old value.
**Risks:** None — tag changes are non-destructive and instantly reversible.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Reconcile the misleading EFA cluster tag
**Description:** The ParallelCluster tag parallelcluster:networking: EFA=NONE contradicts the actual launch template (lt-025a88cbeaba7b869), which provisions 8 of 8 efa-only network interfaces on every GPU node. Update the cluster configuration/tag so it accurately reflects that EFA is enabled.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Cluster-level EFA tag/config matches the launch template's actual network interface definitions
- No remaining reference in cluster config or tags claims EFA is disabled when it is not

#### 2. Close the GPU/network/application observability gap
**Description:** No NCCL debug output, CWAgent EFA counters, DCGM GPU metrics, or application/dataloader logs were available during this investigation, preventing confirmation of the exact upstream cause of GPU starvation.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO (with NET/INIT/P2P subsystems) is enabled and shipped to CloudWatch Logs for the next multi-node run
- CWAgent publishes efa_* counters and DCGM GPU metrics for all compute nodes
- Application-level dataloader metrics (batch time, queue depth, worker CPU) are shipped to CloudWatch

#### 3. Investigate the dataloader/application pipeline as the leading suspect
**Description:** GPUs ran at ~0.01% power utilization for the entire captured run while storage and network were both idle/unsaturated, indicating the GPUs were starved of work by something upstream — most likely the data-loading or application layer.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Dataloader prefetch queue depth and batch generation time are measured on the next run
- A root cause (or further elimination) for the GPU starvation is identified using the new instrumentation

**1. Reconcile the misleading EFA cluster tag**

The ParallelCluster tag parallelcluster:networking: EFA=NONE contradicts the actual launch template (lt-025a88cbeaba7b869), which provisions 8 of 8 efa-only network interfaces on every GPU node. Update the cluster configuration/tag so it accurately reflects that EFA is enabled.

Acceptance criteria:
- Cluster-level EFA tag/config matches the launch template's actual network interface definitions
- No remaining reference in cluster config or tags claims EFA is disabled when it is not

**2. Close the GPU/network/application observability gap**

No NCCL debug output, CWAgent EFA counters, DCGM GPU metrics, or application/dataloader logs were available during this investigation, preventing confirmation of the exact upstream cause of GPU starvation.

Acceptance criteria:
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO (with NET/INIT/P2P subsystems) is enabled and shipped to CloudWatch Logs for the next multi-node run

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### GPU training throughput slowdown on distributed-training-triage-b200
**Description:** Training throughput was reported gradually degrading over several days on AWS ParallelCluster distributed-training-triage-b200 (FSx for Lustre fs-077c776983688ad76, us-west-2). GPU compute nodes (i-0be6193831c898671, i-0014ff22f2e2f180f) ran at ~0.01% power utilization — healthy but starved of work — rather than showing compute saturation. No GPU compute node has run on this cluster since ~2026-09-27 11:00Z.
**Time:** 2026-09-24T18:00:00Z - 2026-09-27T11:00:00Z

## Findings

### Hypothesis: FSx for Lustre storage saturation
**Description:** FSx for Lustre fs-077c776983688ad76 (SCRATCH_2, 1200 GiB, ~234 MB/s aggregate throughput budget) was investigated as a candidate bottleneck for the GPU training slowdown. Across the full 72h slowdown window (2026-09-28T18:00Z–2026-10-01T18:30Z) and the preceding 7 days, all FSx utilization metrics stayed near zero: NetworkThroughputUtilization peaked at 1.02% (typical ~0.5%), FileServerDiskThroughputUtilization peaked at 5.66% (median ~0.03%), DiskIopsUtilization (metadata) peaked at 0.12%. DataReadBytes/DataWriteBytes were negligible (~4KB/5min) throughout the slowdown window, aside from a single one-time staging burst at 2026-09-24 18:00Z (~70.9 GB read + ~70.9 GB write in that hour, ~39 MB/s aggregate, ~17% of budget) that occurred well before the slowdown window and is unrelated to it. FreeDataStorageCapacity stayed flat (~1.166 TB free), MetadataOperations showed no storm, and the Thursday 11:30 UTC weekly maintenance window showed no data gaps or dips. No saturated metric exists anywhere in the window.
**Cascades to:** symptom-training-slowdown

#### Gaps
- **CloudTrail access unavailable:** cloudtrail lookup_events is blocked in this environment ("cloudtrail service operations are not allowed"), preventing reconstruction of the exact RunInstances/TerminateInstances timeline for the GPU fleet on the distributed-training-triage-b200 ParallelCluster. The investigation is relying on CloudWatch metrics (e.g. GPUPowerUtilization per instance) and log group streams (kernel, gpu-health, slurm) instead to infer node lifecycle and concurrency.

### Hypothesis: Network/EFA misconfiguration causing slowdown
**Description:** Investigated whether the ParallelCluster tag `EFA=NONE` meant EFA was disabled and causing NCCL to fall back to slow TCP transport. Found the GPU compute launch template (lt-025a88cbeaba7b869, both default v1 and latest v4) actually provisions the full 8 of 8 EFA interfaces (NetworkCardIndex 0-7, InterfaceType efa-only) alongside the primary ENA - the cluster tag is misleading/stale. Separately, the only GPU instance active during the slowdown window (i-0ec31e7eff7635265) is not a b200 training node at all - it belongs to an unrelated p6-b300 verification cluster (b300-xid-verify) in a different VPC. No real distributed-training-triage-b200 GPU node has run since ~2026-09-27, meaning there is no multi-node job for inter-node network/EFA/NCCL to bottleneck.
**Cascades to:** symptom-training-slowdown

#### Gaps
- **NCCL transport logging was never enabled:** NCCL_DEBUG was not set during the prior 2-node run (2026-09-24 to 2026-09-27), so no NCCL INFO/WARN lines were ever shipped to logs. It is therefore impossible to confirm which network transport (EFA vs TCP socket fallback) NCCL actually selected for that run, even though EFA was correctly provisioned in the launch template. Recommend enabling NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET,P2P,SHM,NVLS with NCCL_DEBUG_FILE shipped to logs for any future multi-node run, to directly confirm transport selection instead of relying on launch-template inference.

### Hypothesis: GPU hardware fault causing slowdown
**Description:** Investigated whether B200 GPU hardware faults (Xid errors, ECC errors, NVLink faults, thermal throttling) explained the near-idle GPU utilization. Both in-scope B200 nodes (i-0be6193831c898671, i-0014ff22f2e2f180f) reported 8/8 healthy GPUs, zero NVRM Xid/ECC/NVLink/thermal errors, with proven continuous kernel-log coverage across their entire run (2026-09-24 18:00Z to ~2026-09-27 10:00-11:00Z), and no AWS Health events for the region/window.
**Cascades to:** symptom-training-slowdown

#### Gaps
- **CloudTrail access unavailable:** cloudtrail lookup_events is blocked in this environment ("cloudtrail service operations are not allowed"), preventing reconstruction of the exact RunInstances/TerminateInstances timeline for the GPU fleet on the distributed-training-triage-b200 ParallelCluster. The investigation is relying on CloudWatch metrics (e.g. GPUPowerUtilization per instance) and log group streams (kernel, gpu-health, slurm) instead to infer node lifecycle and concurrency.
- **NCCL transport logging was never enabled:** NCCL_DEBUG was not set during the prior 2-node run (2026-09-24 to 2026-09-27), so no NCCL INFO/WARN lines were ever shipped to logs. It is therefore impossible to confirm which network transport (EFA vs TCP socket fallback) NCCL actually selected for that run, even though EFA was correctly provisioned in the launch template. Recommend enabling NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET,P2P,SHM,NVLS with NCCL_DEBUG_FILE shipped to logs for any future multi-node run, to directly confirm transport selection instead of relying on launch-template inference.
- **No application-layer telemetry available:** The cluster shipped no training job/application logs, no NCCL debug output, and no compute-node CPU/dataloader/DCGM metrics — only kernel/bootstrap log streams and AWS/EC2 GPUPowerUtilization. Compute nodes are now terminated, so live inspection is impossible. Confirming the exact upstream (dataloader/application) root cause requires job-level instrumentation on a future run.

### Hypothesis: GPUs starved by upstream data-loading/application pipeline
**Description:** With storage (FSx fs-077c776983688ad76), network/EFA, and GPU hardware all cleared with measured evidence, the GPUs sat at ~0.01% power utilization for nearly the entire 2026-09-24→09-27 run — healthy but given no work. This points to a bottleneck upstream of all three subsystems: the CPU-side data-loading pipeline, job orchestration, or the training job never ramping into real work. The dataset was staged to FSx once (~71GB) and not read again during the run, consistent with a stalled dataloader or an idle job.
**Cascades to:** symptom-training-slowdown

#### Gaps
- **No application-layer telemetry available:** The cluster shipped no training job/application logs, no NCCL debug output, and no compute-node CPU/dataloader/DCGM metrics — only kernel/bootstrap log streams and AWS/EC2 GPUPowerUtilization. Compute nodes are now terminated, so live inspection is impossible. Confirming the exact upstream (dataloader/application) root cause requires job-level instrumentation on a future run.

     22	
     23	# GPU Cluster Evidence, Readiness, and Fault Verdicts
     24	
     25	For GPU clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or EKS), AWS ParallelCluster, and self-managed
     26	EC2 or EKS. Generic investigation finds the obvious signals; this skill adds what it gets
     27	wrong: silent evidence, wrong-headline hardware verdicts, and predictable failures before a
     28	long run. **Read-only.** Never reboot, replace, update, or delete anything, and never read
     29	training data, checkpoints, or model weights.
     30	
     31	## Critical rules R1 to R10 (apply in every mode, in this order)
     32	
     33	R1. **Answer in one pass, and always leave room to answer.** In chat, do not stop to ask a
     34	   question and do not hand off to a separate investigation before answering. If an input is
     35	   missing, use the default (impact window: last 24 hours; run length: evaluate 24, 48, and
     36	   72 hours), state the assumption, and mark dependent checks `Needs input`. For "slow" or
     37	   performance questions with no time given, use the last 72 hours. Offer follow-ups only
     38	   after the answer.
     39	   **Budget the evidence gathering so the answer always gets written.** An investigation that
     40	   runs out of room before it reports is worth nothing to the operator, and it is worse than a
     41	   partial answer because it looks like a failure rather than a finding. So: collect the
     42	   mandatory evidence for the mode first (R2, R4, R5, and for Mode P the P1 to P6 core), then
     43	   write the report. Pick up the optional checks only with what is left. If you notice you are
     44	   deep into tool calls and have not yet produced an answer, **stop collecting and report what
     45	   you have**, marking everything unreached as `Not checked` with the call that would close
     46	   it. Never end a turn with evidence gathered and no verdict.
     47	R2. **Inventory and capability profile.** HyperPod: `sagemaker.DescribeCluster` and
     48	   `ListClusterNodes` (paginate). Read `NodeProvisioningMode` from `DescribeCluster`: if it is
     49	   `Continuous`, also pull `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` for the window (see rule R11), which
     50	   is the only timeline source that survives broken log delivery. On any other value the call
     51	   is unsupported and must be skipped, not retried.
     52	   EC2/ParallelCluster/EKS: `ec2.DescribeInstances`. For every
     53	   GPU instance type: `ec2.DescribeInstanceTypes` (strip HyperPod `ml.`): GPU count,
     54	   `EfaSupported`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces`; per EC2 node, attached `efa`/`efa-only` interfaces.
     55	   Report `<attached> of <max>`, where attached = interfaces with `InterfaceType` `efa` or

     57	   are not visible to `DescribeInstances`: say so. On NVSwitch types, search every log source

     60	   gives the node a **new instance ID in the same instance group**, so the current ID will
     61	   never appear in the replace request. Query CloudTrail **by event name, not by instance
     62	   ID**: `cloudtrail.LookupEvents` with `LookupAttributes=[{AttributeKey: EventName,
     63	   AttributeValue: BatchReplaceClusterNodes}]`, then again for `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     64	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `UpdateCluster`, with `StartTime` = window start minus 6

     67	   that is not in the current `ListClusterNodes` output was replaced; the instance group
     68	   whose node has a `LaunchTime` just after that event is the replaced group. That operator

     71	   `logGroupNamePattern` (case-sensitive substring) = the cluster name, then again for
     72	   `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`, `journal`, and `gpu`, paginating with `nextToken`. Never

     76	   carries `kernel:` lines, then bin **that exact stream** by hour across the window padded by

     39	   **Budget the evidence gathering so the answer always gets written.** An investigation that
     40	   runs out of room before it reports is worth nothing to the operator, and it is worse than a
     41	   partial answer because it looks like a failure rather than a finding. So: collect the
     42	   mandatory evidence for the mode first (R2, R4, R5, and for Mode P the P1 to P6 core), then
     43	   write the report. Pick up the optional checks only with what is left. If you notice you are
     44	   deep into tool calls and have not yet produced an answer, **stop collecting and report what
     45	   you have**, marking everything unreached as `Not checked` with the call that would close
     46	   it. Never end a turn with evidence gathered and no verdict.
     47	R2. **Inventory and capability profile.** HyperPod: `sagemaker.DescribeCluster` and
     48	   `ListClusterNodes` (paginate). Read `NodeProvisioningMode` from `DescribeCluster`: if it is
     49	   `Continuous`, also pull `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` for the window (see rule R11), which
     50	   is the only timeline source that survives broken log delivery. On any other value the call
     51	   is unsupported and must be skipped, not retried.
     52	   EC2/ParallelCluster/EKS: `ec2.DescribeInstances`. For every
     53	   GPU instance type: `ec2.DescribeInstanceTypes` (strip HyperPod `ml.`): GPU count,
     54	   `EfaSupported`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces`; per EC2 node, attached `efa`/`efa-only` interfaces.
     55	   Report `<attached> of <max>`, where attached = interfaces with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     56	   `efa-only` (the primary ENA interface does not count unless it is `efa`). HyperPod nodes
     57	   are not visible to `DescribeInstances`: say so. On NVSwitch types, search every log source
     58	   found under rule R4 for `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` before saying it is not confirmed.
     59	R3. **Node identity survives replacement.** A HyperPod reboot keeps the instance ID; a replace
     60	   gives the node a **new instance ID in the same instance group**, so the current ID will
     61	   never appear in the replace request. Query CloudTrail **by event name, not by instance
     62	   ID**: `cloudtrail.LookupEvents` with `LookupAttributes=[{AttributeKey: EventName,
     63	   AttributeValue: BatchReplaceClusterNodes}]`, then again for `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     64	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `UpdateCluster`, with `StartTime` = window start minus 6
     65	   hours and `EndTime` = now as full ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, paginating with `NextToken`.
     66	   Keep events whose `requestParameters.clusterName` is this cluster. A `nodeIds` entry
     67	   that is not in the current `ListClusterNodes` output was replaced; the instance group
     68	   whose node has a `LaunchTime` just after that event is the replaced group. That operator
     69	   or automatic call is the explanation for the node going `Pending` (Branch E), not hardware.
     70	R4. **Find every log source by substring, not prefix.** Call `logs.DescribeLogGroups` with
     71	   `logGroupNamePattern` (case-sensitive substring) = the cluster name, then again for
     72	   `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`, `journal`, and `gpu`, paginating with `nextToken`. Never
     73	   search only `/aws/parallelcluster` or `/aws/sagemaker` prefixes: customer pipelines use
     74	   other names (for example `/aws/<pipeline>/<cluster>/kernel`). Evaluate every source found.
     75	R5. **Prove coverage before any "no errors".** For each node and source: find the stream that
     76	   carries `kernel:` lines, then bin **that exact stream** by hour across the window padded by
     77	   one hour. **Always name the evidence you used: quote the full log group name and the exact
     78	   log stream name for every node in the coverage table, and again in the answer text.** A
     79	   coverage claim without the group and stream it rests on is not auditable, so the operator
     80	   cannot re-run it. Any empty hour means `Not observable` for that hour. First and last event times
     81	   are not proof, and the time of the **last `kernel:` line** is not when logging stopped:
     82	   a healthy kernel goes quiet. Liveness comes only from the hourly bins of all lines in
     83	   that stream. A node is `Measured` if one source passes. HyperPod: a missing
     84	   `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<group>/<instance-id>` stream means `No HMA detections`
     85	   when the cluster log group is otherwise live. NCCL transport with no `NCCL INFO` lines
     86	   anywhere is `Not observable`; never infer it from the instance type.
     87	R5a. **Name every resource you looked at, by ID.** A finding the operator cannot re-run is
     88	   not a finding. Whatever you analysed, put its identifier in the answer: the FSx file system
     89	   (`fs-...`) behind any storage claim, the instance IDs (`i-...`) behind any node claim, the
     90	   cluster name, the capacity reservation (`cr-...`) behind any capacity claim, and the log
     91	   group and stream behind any log claim as R5 already requires. "The file system was
     92	   saturated" or "the metrics looked fine" names nothing and cannot be checked. This applies
     93	   to the resource you cleared as much as the one you blamed, since ruling something out is
     94	   only useful if the reader knows what was ruled out.
     95	R6. **Verdict per node, headline to match.** `REPLACE`, `REBOOT`, `LEAVE ALONE`, `MONITOR`, or
     96	   `NOT OBSERVABLE`, against the evidence bar in `references/incident-branches.md` (Step 4b).
     97	   Application-class Xids (for example 13, 31) or HMA `reason: XidUserAppError` with the node
     98	   `Running` is `LEAVE ALONE`. Never headline "hardware error" unless the verdict is `REPLACE`
     99	   or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds.
     100	R7. **Label every cause** `Proven` (measured signal on the affected node, before the failure,
     101	   nothing competing) or `Hypothesis (to validate)` with the one confirming measurement. A
     102	   spike at the same time is correlation. FSx without a saturated metric is not a proven cause.
     103	   Only a `Proven` cause may be called the root cause, in the headline or in a branch table.
     104	   Otherwise write `Leading hypothesis: <cause>`, or `Root cause: Not observable` when the
     105	   deciding evidence is missing (for example a dead control-plane log). Never write "Proven
     106	   mechanism" for something whose trigger or removal path you did not observe.
     107	   Utilization metrics from FSx (`NetworkThroughputUtilization`, `DiskIopsUtilization`, and
     108	   similar) and `GPUPowerUtilization` are already percent from 0 to 100: a value of `0.9` is
     109	   0.9 percent. Quote the raw value with a percent sign.
     110	R8. **Recovery questions** always state three things: whether automatic node recovery is on
     111	   (`NodeRecovery`), what it does (reboot or replace the node), and that the **job** resumes
     112	   only with checkpoints plus the orchestrator's auto-resume (Slurm on HyperPod:
     113	   `srun --auto-resume=1`).
     114	R9. **Capacity Blocks** begin terminating instances 30 minutes before the end time (60 for
     115	   UltraServers); blocks end at 11:30 UTC and termination starts at 11:00 UTC on the last day.
     116	   For a planned run, write out: usable until = end time minus the lead time; run end = start
     117	   plus run length; hours covered = usable until minus start. Give every value as a full UTC
     118	   date and time, and check the latest safe start is not already in the past.
     119	R10. **Rule out the frequent non-GPU causes** in `references/cluster-edge-cases.md` before
     120	   blaming hardware: subnet IP or network interface exhaustion, ParallelCluster bootstrap
     121	   failures and protected mode, EFA nodes in a public subnet, a Capacity Block not yet
     122	   active, and the FSx maintenance window. HyperPod does not export system metrics to
     123	   CloudWatch, so HyperPod GPU activity is `Not observable` there.
     124	R11. **When the logs are dead, ask the control plane.** On a HyperPod cluster with
     125	   `NodeProvisioningMode = Continuous`, `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` gives you a node and
     126	   cluster timeline that owes nothing to a log agent, so it keeps answering when a stream has
     127	   gone silent or a node has disappeared. Filter the window with `EventTimeAfter` and
     128	   `EventTimeBefore`, narrow with `NodeId` or `InstanceGroupName`, sort with
     129	   `SortBy=EventTime`, and page through `NextToken`. Where a `Description` is not
     130	   self-explanatory, `DescribeClusterEvent` has the detail. Note that the response has no
     131	   severity or level field at all, so any grouping you apply is your own and should be
     132	   described that way. If `NodeProvisioningMode` is anything other than `Continuous` the call
     133	   is not supported; write `ListClusterEvents not supported` in the coverage table and carry
     134	   on. What you must not do is report a dead log as "no events" without either trying this
     135	   source or saying it was unavailable.

{"id": "321e054e-363b-4be4-b84f-0d375b55869c", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_kMEEKq0Zx9v7XwFjEEjdrg", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Signals and Thresholds
     2	
     3	Thresholds here are investigation heuristics for flagging a signal as worth reporting.
     4	They are not AWS service limits. State the observed value, not only the label.
     5	
     6	## HyperPod node state
     7	
     8	Valid `InstanceStatus.Status` values
     9	([ClusterInstanceStatusDetails](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/APIReference/API_ClusterInstanceStatusDetails.html)):
     10	`Running | Failure | Pending | ShuttingDown | SystemUpdating | DeepHealthCheckInProgress | NotFound`.
     11	
     12	| Signal | Flag when |
     13	|--------|-----------|
     14	| Node in `Failure` | Always. Correlate with HMA log for that instance. |
     15	| Node in `Pending` | Longer than 30 minutes: replacement or launch blocked. Check capacity and `LifecycleConfig` logs. |
     16	| Node in `DeepHealthCheckInProgress` | Well past 2 hours. DCGM level 4 alone typically takes about 45 to 90 minutes, and the stress, EFA, and NCCL tests add to it. Check `DeepHealthCheckResults/<id>` streams first |
     17	| `CurrentCount < TargetCount` | Persisting across two inventory reads. |
     18	| `NodeRecovery = None` | Always report. Automatic reboot or replace is disabled. |
     19	| `CurrentImageId != DesiredImageId` | Software update in progress or stalled. |
     20	
     21	## FSx for Lustre (`AWS/FSx`)
     22	
     23	Metric semantics and dimensions:
     24	[FSx for Lustre metrics and dimensions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/fs-metrics.html).
     25	
     26	| Metric (dimensions) | Stat | Flag when | Meaning |
     27	|---------------------|------|-----------|---------|
     28	| `NetworkThroughputUtilization` (FileSystemId, FileServer) | Maximum | ≥ 90% sustained 5+ min | File server network throughput saturated |
     29	| `FileServerDiskThroughputUtilization` (FileSystemId, FileServer) | Maximum | ≥ 90% sustained 5+ min | OSS-to-disk throughput saturated |
     30	| `DiskIopsUtilization` (FileSystemId, StorageTargetId) | Maximum | ≥ 90% sustained 5+ min | OST IOPS saturated (not on Scratch or Persistent HDD) |
     31	| `CPUUtilization` (FileSystemId, FileServer = MDS*) | Maximum | ≥ 90% sustained 5+ min | Metadata server saturated |
     32	| `MetadataOperations` (FileSystemId) | Sum / period | Sharp rise aligned with the slowdown | Metadata-heavy workload |
     33	| `FreeDataStorageCapacity` (FileSystemId, StorageTargetId) | Minimum per OST | Any OST < 10% free while others have space | Imbalanced striping, write failures possible |
     34	| `DataReadBytes` + `DataWriteBytes` (FileSystemId) | Sum / period | Drop aligned with the stall | Clients stopped doing I/O (effect, not cause) |
     35	
     36	Throughput in bytes per second is `Sum / period_seconds`. Do not report raw `Sum` as a
     37	rate.
     38	
     39	A drop in client I/O during a hang is usually the **effect** of the job stalling. It
     40	points at storage only if a saturation metric above rose first.
     41	
     42	## GPU activity
     43	
     44	`AWS/EC2` `GPUPowerUtilization` (dimensions `InstanceId` and `GpuId`, as observed in live
     45	accounts; the EC2 docs list the metric but not the `GpuId` dimension) is published by EC2 for a
     46	subset of accelerated instance types without an agent. Unit is Percent of maximum active
     47	power ([EC2 accelerator metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/viewing_metrics_with_cloudwatch.html#accelerator-metrics)).
     48	
     49	| Signal | Flag when |
     50	|--------|-----------|
     51	| Every GPU on a node below 5% power for an hour | Idle hour (heuristic). On reserved capacity, count it as an idle reserved hour |
     52

NCCL TRANSPORT from logs: search the cluster/job logs (DescribeLogGroups by substring: cluster name, "nccl", "gpu", "messages", "syslog") for NCCL INFO lines showing the transport in use — NET/IB or NET/OFI/EFA (good) versus NET/Socket (TCP fallback = slow inter-node). No NCCL lines anywhere = Not observable; do not infer transport from the instance type.
5. RULE OUT network edge cases (skill R10): subnet IP / ENI exhaustion in subnet-024dbe437aef9d7eb (describe the subnet's available IP count and ENIs), EFA nodes placed in a public subnet, security-group rules required for EFA/NCCL. 
6. If EFA counters are available (CWAgent EFA metrics like rdma rx/tx, retransmits), pull them for the window.

Report: a clear verdict on whether the network was a bottleneck. State the EFA interface count ("<attached> of <max>"), whether the job was single- or multi-node, the NCCL transport actually observed (or Not observable), and subnet/ENI headroom. Be explicit: if single-node, network/EFA is NOT the cause; if multi-node without EFA, quantify the likely inter-node bandwidth impact. Label causes `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)`.
